Q: Tab grouping and tab colouring: How to get this feature to tabs opened from my web page irrespective of browser A:

One distinction that might help future readers: “tab grouping” and “tab coloring” solve slightly different problems.

Grouping organizes tabs structurally, but when you have many tabs that look identical, coloring individual tabs (often per domain) can be a faster way to visually identify what you’re switching to-which is why some people prefer that approach via extensions.

Q: Why does Matplotlib DatetimeIndex plot misalign dates? A:

This is actually a pandas issue, not matplotlib. There are a couple issues still open on GitHub (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/11574) that span back quite some time.

If you avoid the pandas.Series.plot and pandas.DataFrame.plot interfaces then you'll end up with a more consistent result (left column is plotted through pandas, right column is plotted directly through matplotlib):

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from datetime import date

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=4, ncols=2, figsize=(10, 8), layout="constrained")

# --
axes[0, 0].set_title("pandas\nMonth ends first")
pd.Series([0, 2, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[0, 0], c="b")
pd.Series([0, 1, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[0, 0], c="r")

axes[0, 1].set_title("matplotlib\nMonth ends first")
axes[0, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 2, 0], c="b")
axes[0, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 1, 0], c="r")

# --
axes[1, 0].set_title("Middle of month first")
pd.Series([0, 1, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[1, 0], c="r")
pd.Series([0, 2, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[1, 0], c="b")

axes[1, 1].set_title("Middle of month first")
axes[1, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 1, 0], c="r")
axes[1, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 2, 0], c="b")

# --
axes[2, 0].set_title("Not end of month first")
pd.Series([0, 2, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-28", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[2, 0], c="b")
pd.Series([0, 1, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[2, 0], c="r")

axes[2, 1].set_title("Not end of month first")
axes[2, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-28", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 2, 0], c="b")
axes[2, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 1, 0], c="r")

# --
axes[3, 0].set_title("Not end of month first fence post")
pd.Series([0, 2, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-27", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[3, 0], c="b")
pd.Series([0, 1, 0], pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"])).plot(ax=axes[3, 0], c="r")

axes[3, 1].set_title("Not end of month first fence post")
axes[3, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-27", "2025-12-31", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 2, 0], c="b")
axes[3, 1].plot(pd.DatetimeIndex(["2025-11-30", "2025-12-15", "2026-01-31"]), [0, 1, 0], c="r")

# clean up the x-axis on the "pure" matplotlib charts
from matplotlib.dates import AutoDateLocator
from matplotlib.dates import ConciseDateFormatter
for ax in axes[:, 1]:
    locator = AutoDateLocator()
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(locator)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(ConciseDateFormatter(locator))

from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
fig.add_artist(Line2D([.525, .525], [0, 1], transform=fig.transFigure, color='k'))

plt.show()

Q: How accurate is the == function with floats with different decimals A:

How accurate is the == function with floats with different decimals

float a == b is an exact value comparison. Either a,b have the same value or not.

(+0.0, -0.0 and NaN have additional concerns).

Rather than thinking of float as having decimals, view that a float is some limited ranged integer times some limited ranged power-of-2.

I suspect OP's true concern is more like "How accurate is float"?
Recall float is a floating point. For float, precision is typically about 1 part in 224. The absolute precision varies with the magnitude. It steps with each power-of-2 such that 200000.0f/7.0f is about relatively precise as 0.02f/7.0f.

I have multiplied the result of the value on the right side of the equality above by 10, ...
I work with increments of + 0.1.
1 * 1e6

float, double are commonly base-2 floating point types. When trying to form an integer like operation, scale these types by 2.
Work in increments that are a power-of-2.
0x1.0p10

printf("k6 = %f and k7 = %f.", i, k);

Instead of print in decimal, use "%a" to see the significand in hexadecimal.

float C1 = -2783.02, C2 = -3921.87, ....

Avoid mixing double (constants and functions) and float (objects). Best to use 1 floating type like double throughout or perhaps float. E.g.: float C1 = -2783.02f. It sometimes makes a difference.

If it is not possible to eliminate the garbage error on the counter x, how can I be sure that the equality is met?

The equality might not have a solution as floating point numbers are a subset of real numbers.

Code might, though, get to a minimal difference of a few ULP. A variation on ULP_diff() may work for OP, yet there is a lot of analysis needed to truly solve OP's goal.
